paras: The Cambridge Uncle Tom's Cabin disturbance was a disorder in Cambridge, Maryland, in early July 1903 or shortly before, following a traveling company's performance of "Uncle Tom's Cabin." A Montgomery, Alabama, editorial said it ended with "a number" of Black residents beaten, though no attackers were named. The episode reached the press only as a reason Maryland officials gave for barring the same play from two other Eastern Shore towns.

In July 1903 a theatrical company touring "Uncle Tom's Cabin" was licensed to play Berlin and Snow Hill in Worcester County, Maryland. After a protest the license was revoked, on the ground that "the recent outrage and lynching of a negro in Delaware" had inflamed the Eastern Shore and that the play would not serve "peace and good order" in counties with large Black populations.

The only account of Cambridge itself is secondhand: a dispatch from Berlin to the Baltimore Sun said "it was stated" that a recent performance there "produced considerable excitement and disorder among the negroes." That dispatch, sent on the night of July 14, gave no date, names or injuries. Three days later the Montgomery Advertiser wrote that the company "got the town of Cambridge into a row a few evenings ago," that the play "acted like incendiarism upon the negroes," and that it "ended in a number of them suffering beatings." Neither report named any attacker.
No arrests, prosecutions or official inquiry into the Cambridge disorder appear in the coverage; its only recorded consequence was its use to justify the Worcester County revocation.

The Berlin dispatch ran in the Washington Evening Star on July 15 under the headline "'UNCLE TOM' BARRED" and on July 16 in the Birmingham Age-Herald and the Louisville Courier-Journal, both inside a Washington special. In each the Cambridge disorder was a single closing sentence, framed as unrest among Black residents rather than as an attack on them.

The Montgomery Advertiser turned the story into an editorial, "Barn Stormers Have Storm," welcoming the "counter storm" against what it called "the miserable libel upon the Southern people and exaltation of the negro." It was the only paper found to mention beatings, and it presented them as the play's doing rather than any attacker's. All of the coverage found was in white papers, none of them from Cambridge.

The two versions differ in what happened: the dispatch, closer to the source, describes only "excitement and disorder among the negroes," while the later Alabama editorial, which names no source, says Black residents were beaten.

accounts.label: Berlin, Md. dispatch to the Baltimore Sun
accounts.gist: Reporting the revocation of the Worcester county license, it said it 'was stated' that a recent performance at Cambridge 'produced considerable excitement and disorder among the negroes'; it mentions no beatings or attackers.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser editorial
accounts.gist: Retelling the same story, it said the company 'got the town of Cambridge into a row' and that the play, acting 'like incendiarism upon the negroes', ended with a number of them beaten.

framing.detail: Headlined '"UNCLE TOM" BARRED' (Evening Star) and 'Uncle Tom's Cabin Co. Is Not Allowed to Play' (Age-Herald); the Cambridge disorder is a one-sentence justification for the revocation, attributed to Black residents' excitement.

The Montgomery Advertiser's 'Barn Stormers Have Storm' welcomed the 'counter storm' against a 'miserable libel upon the Southern people' and presented the beatings as the play's result, not as an assault by anyone.

versions.value: 'considerable excitement and disorder among the negroes'; no violence against anyone described
'a row' that 'ended in a number of them [negroes] suffering beatings'

conflicts.note: Not a contradiction so much as a difference in detail: the earlier dispatch is closer to the source but vaguer; the beatings appear only in a later editorial from Alabama whose source is not given.

record_check.dossier: No attack on the Black community as a whole is described; one editorial reports 'a number' of Black residents beaten in a 'row' (coded mob_assault, weakly); the dispatch reports only disorder among Black residents.
Before July 14, 1903 (called 'recent' in a dispatch of the night of July 14); possibly late June or early July.
No county is named for Cambridge in the coverage.
Black ('a number of them', referring to 'the negroes'), per the Montgomery Advertiser only.
At least three white papers carried the Cambridge sentence, the first on July 15 (Evening Star), before the Montgomery editorial.
Weak: one secondhand dispatch sentence plus one editorial; no local or Black-press report found.
